segments.text: Every clock you've ever looked at is secretly copying a shadow. That's why clock hands turn the way they do.
Push a stick into the ground anywhere north of the equator. The sun rises in the east, swings across the southern sky, and sets in the west.
So the stick's shadow sweeps the opposite way. West in the morning, north at noon, east by evening. Left, top, right. Clockwise.
For thousands of years, sundials were the clock. So when the first mechanical clocks rose in European towers in the {1300s,|thirteen hundreds,} their makers simply copied the shadow.
Here's the twist. Build that sundial in Australia, and the shadow turns the other way. If clocks had been invented down south, clockwise would mean the opposite.
And a few clocks still rebel. The clock Paolo Uccello painted for Florence Cathedral in {1443|fourteen forty-three} runs backwards. So does the Hebrew clock on Prague's Jewish Town Hall.
So next time you check the time, remember: you're really reading a shadow. If you enjoyed this, like and follow for more.
